title: Who holds the leash
hook: whoever controls what you want is your master (Enchiridion 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday: content to seem foolish. Your line was let them think it. Did you ask the obvious question, or say I don't know, and survive it? Day three hundred forty-six.

A phone buzzes on a table. Three people at dinner glance at it, including the person who swore they weren't going to. Somewhere, someone who designed that buzz is very pleased. Here's a strange way to measure freedom. Not by what you're allowed to do, but by how many hands can tug you. If anyone who can give or withhold what you badly want can move you, then they have a kind of leash on you. Epictetus, who spent his youth legally owned by another man, thought about this more carefully than most. Today: who holds the leash.
screen: `THE PHONE BUZZES.` → `HOW MANY HANDS CAN TUG YOU?` → `WHO HOLDS THE LEASH.`

segments.voice: First, the foolish wish. Section fourteen opens bluntly. If you want your children and your partner and your friends to live forever, Epictetus says, you're being foolish: you want things that aren't up to you to be up to you. If you want other people never to make mistakes, same problem. He isn't saying don't love them. He's saying don't demand what no one can promise. Second, the definition. Then comes the line the index gives us. Each person's master, he says, is whoever has the power to give or take away what that person wants or wants to avoid. That's the leash. Not chains. Wanting. Third, the way out. So whoever wants to be free, he says, should neither want nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, he says, that person is bound to be a slave. It's a severe word, and he chose it knowing exactly what it meant. Fourth, the leashes we hold out ourselves. Look at what tugs a modern day: a boss's approval, a crush's reply, likes on a post, a parent's praise, a number on a scale. None of those people or things are bad. But each time we let our peace depend on them, we hand someone the end of a leash, usually without their asking. Epictetus' point is that a lot of these leashes can be let go of from our end. We can still want the reply. We can just stop needing it. The person holding the other end may never notice. You will.
screen: `DON'T DEMAND WHAT NO ONE CAN PROMISE.` · `YOUR MASTER: WHOEVER HOLDS WHAT YOU WANT.` · `WANT NOTHING THAT DEPENDS ON OTHERS.` · `THE LEASHES WE HAND OVER.` · then, large: `WHO HOLDS THE LEASH?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture your day as a field, with a few leashes trailing from you. Notice where they lead. To a phone. To a person's opinion. To a number. Choose one. Follow it to whoever holds the other end. Ask: what do I want from them that they can give or withhold? Don't cut it yet. Just loosen your own grip on it, a little, and feel the slack. The bell holds the time.
Who holds the leash. Epictetus' measure of freedom: whoever controls what you want or fear is your master, until you let that want go. Today's word.
Your line: who holds the leash. When something tugs you today, a buzz, a look, a number, ask the question, and loosen your end. Day three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism notice which wants make them dependent on others, such as approval or replies, and practice wanting them less urgently.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 14: master, the one with authority.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't let people boss you around.
what it means: whoever holds what you want can move you; freedom is wanting nothing that depends on them.
what a scholar hears: kyrios, master; for a man born into slavery, freedom (eleutheria) became the theme running through all his teaching.

notes: Enchiridion 14 paraphrased (children, wife, friends to live forever; slave without faults; 'the master of each man is he who has the power over the things which he wishes or does not wish'; whoever would be free). Confirm.
Eleutheria as a central theme (e.g. Discourses 4.1, 'On Freedom'): confirm phrasing in trapdoor.
The leash image is the index's, not the text's; the phone and likes are modern illustrations.
